segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Paul, a slave of Christ Jesus, called to be an apostle, set apart for the good news of God,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: which he promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: concerning his Son, who was born a descendant of David according to the flesh,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: who was appointed Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness by resurrection from the dead—Jesus Christ our Lord,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: through whom we received grace and apostleship to bring about the obedience of faith among all the Gentiles for the sake of his name,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: among whom you also are called to belong to Jesus Christ—

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: to all in Rome who are loved by God, called to be holy ones: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: First, I thank my God through Jesus Christ for all of you, because your faith is being proclaimed in the whole world.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For God, whom I serve in my spirit in the good news of his Son, is my witness how unceasingly I make mention of you

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: always in my prayers, asking that somehow, now at last, I may succeed by God’s will in coming to you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For I long to see you, so that I may share with you some spiritual gift to strengthen you—

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: that is, that we may be encouraged together while I am among you, through one another’s faith, both yours and mine.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I do not want you to be unaware, brothers and sisters, that I have often planned to come to you—and have been prevented until now—so that I might have some fruit among you too, just as among the rest of the Gentiles.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I am a debtor both to Greeks and to barbarians, both to the wise and to the foolish;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so, for my part, I am eager to proclaim the good news to you also who are in Rome.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For I am not ashamed of the good news, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For in it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith to faith, as it is written:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “The righteous will live by faith.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all the ungodliness and unrighteousness of people who suppress the truth by their unrighteousness,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: because what can be known about God is plain among them, for God has made it plain to them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For since the creation of the world, what is unseen of him—his eternal power and divine nature—has been clearly seen, being understood through the things he has made, so that they are without excuse,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: because, though they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give him thanks; instead they became futile in their reasoning, and their senseless hearts were darkened.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Claiming to be wise, they became fools,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and exchanged the glory of the immortal God for the likeness of an image of a mortal human being, and of birds and four-footed animals and creeping things.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Therefore God handed them over, in the desires of their hearts, to impurity, to the dishonoring of their bodies among themselves,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: since they exchanged the truth of God for the lie, and revered and served the creation rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever. Amen.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For this reason God handed them over to dishonorable passions. For their females exchanged natural relations for those contrary to nature,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and likewise the males too, leaving natural relations with the female, burned in their craving for one another, males with males committing shameful acts and receiving in themselves the due penalty for their error.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And just as they did not see fit to acknowledge God, God handed them over to an unfit mind, to do what ought not to be done.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They have been filled with every kind of unrighteousness, wickedness, greed, and malice. They are full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, and spite. They are gossips,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: slanderers, God-haters, insolent, arrogant, boastful, inventors of evil, disobedient to parents,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: senseless, faithless, heartless, merciless.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Though they know God’s righteous decree, that those who practice such things deserve death, they not only do them but also approve of those who practice them.

notes.note: The Greek word is the ordinary term for a slave, a person owned by a master, and Paul applies it to himself in relation to Christ. Most English versions soften it to “servant,” and some scholars also hear an echo of the Old Testament’s honorific “servant of the Lord.” The plain sense of ownership and total allegiance is kept here.

Traditionally “gospel,” which is now a religious term or the name of a book. The Greek was an ordinary word for a public announcement of good news, used also of imperial proclamations. Many modern translations alternate between “gospel” and “good news.”

Many English versions have “declared,” which suggests that the resurrection only made known what Jesus already was. In the usage of the period the verb means to appoint, designate or fix, and most lexicons and recent commentators render it that way here. “In power” may go with “Son of God” (installed as Son of God in power, a new stage for one already called God’s Son in verse 3) or with “appointed” (powerfully appointed).

The phrase occurs only here in the New Testament and reflects a Hebrew way of saying “Holy Spirit.” Most interpreters take it as God’s Spirit, and it is capitalized accordingly. A minority take it as Jesus’s own holy spirit or divine nature, set against “according to the flesh” in verse 3.

The Greek is as compact as the English and can mean the obedience that consists in faith, the obedience that springs from faith, or both at once. The literal phrase is kept so as not to decide the question. The same phrase returns at the close of the letter (16:26).

The Greek word means “nations” or “peoples,” and in the plural it is the regular Jewish term for the non-Jewish peoples; English uses “Gentiles” and “nations” for the one Greek word. “Among all the nations” is possible here, but Paul’s commission was specifically to non-Jews, and verse 13 uses the same word in that sense.

Traditionally “saints,” which now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue. Paul uses the word for all believers as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint’s language for Israel. Other translations keep “saints” or use “God’s holy people.”

Traditionally “brethren” or “brothers.” The Greek masculine plural was the normal way to address a mixed group of men and women, and Paul is writing to the whole community in Rome. Many recent translations render it this way.

To Greek speakers a “barbarian” was anyone who did not speak Greek or share Greek culture; the word carried cultural condescension but did not mean “savage.” “Greeks and barbarians” was a stock way of saying all humankind from the Greek point of view.

Greek has a single word-family where English has two: “righteous” and “just,” “righteousness” and “justice,” “justify.” The phrase may mean God’s own righteousness, especially his action to set things right, or a right standing that comes from God; interpreters are divided. “Righteousness” is kept because “the justice of God” would suggest punishing justice to a modern reader, though some scholars prefer “justice” or “covenant faithfulness.”

The phrase is compressed and disputed. It may be an idiom of emphasis (“by faith from first to last”), or mean that the revelation starts from faith and leads to faith, or, as some argue, that it moves from God’s or Christ’s faithfulness to human faith. The literal wording leaves these options open.

notes.phrase: The righteous will live by faith
notes.traditional: The just shall live by faith
notes.note: A quotation of Habakkuk 2:4. “By faith” can be attached to “will live,” as here, or to “the righteous” (“the one who is righteous by faith will live”); both readings have strong scholarly support. The Greek phrase behind “by faith” is the same one rendered “from faith” earlier in the verse, and the noun can also mean “faithfulness.”

notes.traditional: gave them up; gave them over
notes.note: Traditionally “gave them up” or “gave them over.” The verb is the ordinary word for transferring someone into another’s custody or power, the same word used in the Gospels for Jesus being handed over to the authorities. It recurs as a refrain in verses 24, 26 and 28: God’s judgment takes the form of leaving people in the grip of what they have chosen.

Most versions have “women” and “men” in verses 26–27. Paul does not use the ordinary words for women and men but the terms “female” and “male,” which many interpreters hear as an echo of the creation account (“male and female he created them,” Genesis 1:27). The rendering keeps that choice of words visible.

notes.traditional: reprobate mind; debased mind; depraved mind
notes.note: Traditionally “reprobate,” “debased” or “depraved” mind. The adjective means failing the test, rejected as unfit, and Paul plays on the related verb just before it: they did not “see fit” to acknowledge God, so God handed them over to a mind that is itself “unfit.” The rendering is chosen to keep that wordplay.

In earlier Greek this rare word normally meant “hated by a god,” and some interpreters take it that way here. Because the other items in the list are vices the people themselves practice, most translations and commentators take it in the active sense, “haters of God.”

This translation normally renders the word “righteous requirement” or “righteous act.” Here its content is not something God requires people to do but his verdict that those who do such things deserve death, so “decree” is used, as in several major versions. The word belongs to the same family as “righteousness” in verse 17.

candidates.reason: Translators split between “slave” and “servant” across the Gospels and letters, and the choice affects Paul’s self-descriptions, the parables and the household codes alike.
The plural address recurs in almost every letter and needs one policy on when it is “brothers and sisters” and when “brothers.”
Paul’s uses range from physical descent to the sphere opposed to the Spirit, and versions vary between “flesh,” “human nature” and “sinful nature.”
It is the negative of the δικαιοσύνη family and versions vary between “unrighteousness,” “injustice” and “wickedness,” which hides the link with “righteousness.”
It recurs across the letters and versions vary between “desire,” “lust” and “passion,” which blurs it with πάθος and ὄρεξις.
